content.title: Trump Accounts vs. 529s for College Saving
content.text: Trump accounts, created in July 2025, are a new tax-advantaged account for children. Investors saving for college should know how they compare to 529 accounts. Trump accounts will go live in July 2026. A Trump account is an account that a family member can choose to create for a child. Annual contributions to the account can reach up to $5,000 annually from taxable sources, such as a parent or an employer. Employer contributions cannot exceed $2,500 and they count toward the $5,000 limit. If that child was born between 2025 and 2028, they qualify for a $1,000 contribution to their Trump account. The $1,000 does not count toward the $5,000 limit. When the child turns 18, the account effectively becomes an IRA. For more on the details of Trump accounts, read here. 529 accounts, on the other hand, are tax-advantaged accounts designed for education expenses. If the funds are used on a qualified expense, the growth on the post-tax contributions are tax-free when withdrawn. Comparison Joel Dickson, the Global Head of Advised Strategies at Vanguard, explains there is really no downside risk to having a Trump account. The account itself opens new ways of receiving funds, such as the $1,000 seed money from the federal government, employer contributions, or contributions from charities. “There is free money for you in Trump accounts that isn’t available in other accounts,” Dickson explains. According to a survey of PSCA members, most employers are not yet interested in making contributions, though that could change over time. About 70% of employers responding to a PSCA survey in September said they were not interested in making contributions to a Trump account, 12% said they were not aware of them, and 18% said they might be interested in the future. Additionally, since Trump accounts become IRAs, that means that they have some utility in saving for a house or saving for retirement that 529s don’t have. However, excess funds in 529s can be rolled into a Roth IRA. However, apart from the additional contribution vectors and early retirement saving, Trump accounts struggle to compete against 529s as it relates to saving for education expenses. 529 accounts are essentially Roth accounts for education expenses. The growth on the after-tax contributions isn’t taxed; whereas for Trump accounts, the growth on post-tax money, as well as both growth and principal on pre-tax money are all taxed as ordinary income. As an explainer from JP Morgan puts it, “A free $1,000 for newborns makes Trump accounts a no-brainer. The bigger question is whether to contribute more. For families with education goals, the best approach may be to invest in a more advantageous 529 plan while using the seed money from a Trump account for establishing an early start to saving for other future needs including the purchase of a home or retirement.” 529s also permit a broader investment range. Trump accounts cannot touch active funds or bonds, unlike 529 investors which can invest broadly. 529 investors can also put everything in a target-date fund (TDF), which are presumably banned in Trump accounts since they virtually always contain a bond allocation. Trump accounts are also limited “primarily” to U.S. equities, though the meaning of “primarily” is still being finalized. Dickson adds however, “we don’t know how these accounts may evolve,” and points out that “529s themselves have evolved over time.”
